doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: On the road with Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers
summary: Figuring out Cavallo's varied show from a tape, a lost-in-the-changes embarrassment in Baltimore, odd gigs, and $150 a week.

bands.name: Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Jimmy Cavallo and the House Rockers.
Oh yeah. I’ll be darned. Okay, and what was that gig like for you?

Oh it was very interesting. Talk about diversity. I played for him a little bit and he said “oh this is great I’m going to give you a reel to reel tape of our show, and I want you to figure it out.” There’s no music, no charts, nothing. “I want you to figure out what we’re doing and we’ll have a rehearsal next Thursday” or whatever, like that. And the gig was guitar, bass and drums, and Jimmy sang and played sax. So the charts were everything from Sinatra charts, the orchestration Basie things, that stuff; to soul rock, because he was a rocker; jazz things like [I Got] Rhythm changes, where he’d just go off honking in © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

the audience for twenty minutes and then we’d get to keep that going; and so I had to figure all of that stuff out and cover as many parts of it as I could as a guitar player, trying to play horn parts and everything, and still keep the rhythm going. So it was kind of interesting. Somehow I got the gig. And my first gig on the road was in Baltimore. And we played this huge club, they had like three floors with a bar on every floor and there were people dancing and it was like a massive type of thing. And there’s kind of a funny war story there, Rhythm changes, as you know, it’s 16 bars and then you’ve got the bridge, and then you go back to 8 bars. Well if you do that three, four, five times, you begin to wonder, have I done the first 16 here, or do I have to go again? Now, Jimmy would like jump off the stage, with his saxophone, and he’d be jamming and playing, and he would hop on to these tables. And people would be drinking. And he’s over there dancing on the tables honking the saxophone at them. Right? And he’s getting further and further and further away from the band. Meanwhile we’re just kind of [scats] and this thing is going on and on and on. And probably about the 20th or 30th chorus, I’m lost. I don’t know where I am. I came in with the bridge at the wrong time or something like that. And somebody yells “no you’re at the wrong spot.” So Jimmy realizes this is a problem, so he decides to come back to the stage, gets on the stage, continues to play, puts his saxophone right into my ear and honks the root, telling me where I should be. Loud. So it was a very hard lesson to learn. Don’t get lost. Keep track of the tune. That was an embarrassing moment. But I did learn a lot from the Cavallo band. We did all kinds of gigs, we played in the Amish country. Imagine playing a jazz gig in Lenox, Pennsylvania or York, Pennsylvania. We did these things. Things like — very strange stuff. We also played Atlantic City and some better gigs. But basically he was a rocker that had blues and jazz roots. And he’s still out there. I think he’s about eighty-something years old and still playing.
Do you remember what you made?
Oh yeah. I think we got like $150 a week. Out of that we had to pay for expenses. We had to pay for rooms, we doubled up, pay for your food.
You know I don’t think I’ve ever met a musician in the early part of their career that got their own motel room.
It finally happened by the time I got some better gigs.
